summary: The Tree diameter calculator turns the circumference, the diameter under-bark (Bark details (single)) and the diameter into diameter (Single-stemmed tree). Think of it as a shortcut for an animal, a plant or a biological process whose scale you want to put into perspective. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Tree diameter calculator work?
sections.html:
The Tree diameter calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports diameter (Single-stemmed tree) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the circumference, the diameter under-bark (Bark details (single)), the diameter (Multi-stemmed tree) and the average bark thickness (Bark details (multi)).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Tree diameter calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Diameter=circumference ÷ PI
Diameter=2 × average bark thickness + diameter under-bark
5th stem circumference=the square root of (-(1st stem circumference ^ 2) − (2nd stem circumference ^ 2) − (3rd stem circumference ^ 2) − (4th stem circumference ^ 2) − (6th stem circumference ^ 2) + (PI ^ 2) × (diameter ^ 2))
Diameter under-bark=(1st stem circumference, average bark thickness)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Circumference = 30 cm, 1st stem circumference = 0 cm, 2nd stem circumference = 0 cm and 3rd stem circumference = 0 cm. The calculator returns Diameter = 9.549 cm.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Diameter = 9.549 cm should be roughly the size you expected from Circumference = 30 cm and 1st stem circumference = 0 cm.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Tree diameter calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Supporting a lesson, a lecture or a field note
  • Putting a biological quantity into a scale you can picture
  • Comparing two organisms, populations or processes
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the circumference, the diameter under-bark (Bark details (single)) and the diameter — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Tree diameter calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns diameter (Single-stemmed tree), derived from the circumference, the diameter under-bark (Bark details (single)) and the diameter. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Tree diameter calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the circumference, the diameter under-bark (Bark details (single)) and the diameter, which is 9 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter circumference in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Circumference opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Diameter = 9.549 cm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Tree diameter calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
